text: System 2.2.1.1 Objective Design a novel air distribution system for a small (<50,000-ft2) commercial building within the climate zone of the stakeholder. 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2.2.1.2 Background On average, Americans spend 87% of their time inside buildings, and IAQ in buildings has a direct effect on human health (Klepeis et al. 2001; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 2025). Buildings can even develop “sick building syndrome,” a situation in which IAQ is so poor that building occupants become ill. In the workplace, this can cause absenteeism and decreased productivity (Joshi 2008). Sick building syndrome is caused by the presence of chemical compounds or pathogens that can affect human health and comfort. These include volatile organic compounds, bacteria, viruses, mold, and dust, as well as internal nuisance odors and the heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide generated by occupants. Even when building owners, architects, and interior designers select and install building materials and interior furnishings with minimal hazardous chemical compounds, IAQ can be an issue. Currently, the most common mitigation strategy is ventilating the building interior with fresh outdoor air. Building codes mandate minimum ventilation thresholds based on occupancy classification and space usage. Buildings need to be healthy, but they also need to be comfortable. Modern HVAC systems keep temperature and humidity levels in the human comfort range and condition the fresh outdoor air to the level required for occupant health. Mechanical engineers and HVAC system designers have the challenge of balancing proper ventilation for occupant health with the need to minimize the energy required for space conditioning. Many air distribution systems use metal ductwork to move conditioned air between the outdoors, the HVAC system and conditioning equipment, and indoor spaces. These systems have many issues that impact energy use, occupant comfort, and IAQ. For example: • Ductwork can leak conditioned air, increasing the energy required to condition the occupied spaces. • Conditioned air can gain or lose heat as it travels through the air distribution system, which wastes energy. • Improper placement of the supply and return air grilles can negatively impact air temperature and quality. For example, if the supply air diffuser is placed near the return air grille, the conditioned air may short-circuit to the return grille and never reach the occupied zone in the room. There is a need for more HVAC system designs that are energy-efficient as well as healthy and comfortable for occupants. 2.2.1.3 Challenge Design a novel air distribution system for a small (<50,000-ft2) commercial building within the climate zone of the stakeholder that will: • Provide proper ventilation to all building occupants • Maintain occupant comfort (temperature and humidity) • Eliminate IAQ hazards • Reduce energy use compared to current systems • Meet the functional needs and code requirements of the commercial building. 6 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
